requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.
verdict_reason: verified high finding(s) backed by receipts: logic-edge-1

checked.what: Existing SourceGenerator tests on head: 168/169 passed, 1 failed
Existing SourceGenerator tests on base: 167/167 passed, 0 failed

product-context: deliberate per ledger, not a defect: Generated code on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets is deliberately left without ExcludeFromCodeCoverage through the #if guard. The requirement says all generated code, but the ledger records no preference and says to follow the requirement, so the guard is not a defect. This was checked and is fine.
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageReceipts.cs: requirement test fails on base (1/1), passes on head (1/1)
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageTfmReceipts.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDuplicateTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 1/1 failed
Regeneration: 219/222 generated files verified by 89 passing snapshot tests on head; 1 head test(s) fail

findings.claim: Every template wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` already exists on .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, with class targets allowed. So projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework, a very common setup for MessagePack libraries, still get undecorated formatters and resolvers. The requirement asks for all generated code to be decorated. The derived criterion only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist, and ledger L7 defers to the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageTfmReceipts.GeneratedTypes_AreExcludedFromCoverage_WhenLegacySymbolDefined("NETSTANDARD2_0") and ("NETFRAMEWORK"). The test runs the generator with that preprocessor symbol defined while the attribute type is resolvable. It fails on head because no generated formatter or resolver carries the attribute.

findings.claim: A user who already wrote [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their own partial resolver declaration (for example `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver][ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] partial class MyResolver {}`, which is the obvious manual workaround for this issue) no longer compiles. The generated partial declaration now adds the same attribute. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has AllowMultiple=false, so the compiler reports CS0579 (duplicate attribute). The template does not check whether the user's declaration already carries the attribute. The same applies to user-declared `[CompositeResolver]` partial classes, via CompositeResolverTemplate.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDuplicateTests.UserResolverAlreadyExcludedFromCoverage_StillCompiles. It passes on base and fails on head with CS0579 in the generated MyNs.MyResolver.g.cs.

findings.claim: The attribute is emitted under `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, but the symbols are defined by the target framework, so a project targeting netstandard2.0 or net4x gets no exclusion. A multi-targeting project compiled for netstandard2.1, net6.0 and later does get it. The requirement says all generated code must be decorated, and the guard also skips netstandard2.0, which still has ExcludeFromCodeCoverage in some SDK setups. Coverage for those targets is silently unchanged. Ledger L7 records no preference on this, so it follows the requirement; the unconditional-versus-conditional scope remains a gap.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate output for a compilation with NETSTANDARD2_0 defined (a netstandard2.0 test project) and confirm the generated formatters carry no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. Then check which target frameworks define System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute, to see if the guard is too broad. On netstandard2.0 the attribute type exists only from the System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis package in some SDKs, so the guard may be too narrow.

findings.claim: The generated files now contain `#if` / `#endif` preprocessor lines that start at column 0 inside nested namespace or type emission. In the formatter, enum, union and string-key templates the `#if` lines sit directly after emitted nesting content, so any template that emits no preceding newline could place `#if` mid-line and break compilation. In FormatterTemplate.cs the `this.Write("#if ...` follows `this.Write("\r\n")`, so it is fine there. In StringKeyFormatterTemplate.cs and UnionTemplate.cs the previous write is the nesting-emitter output with no explicit newline, so the `#if` could be glued onto the end of the previous line, such as an opening `{` of a nested type or namespace. Preprocessor directives must be the first token on their line.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests and compile the generated output for a nested-type string-key formatter and a union inside a nested class. Confirm the `#if` begins on its own line and the output compiles. The changed lines were previously `\tinternal sealed class`, so the prior output needed no newline guarantee.

findings.claim: The test only compares generated text and never verifies that the generated code compiles with the attribute on a target framework where it exists, such as a net8.0 compilation with zero diagnostics. A misplaced attribute, for example before a using or an EmitNestingTypes boundary, or on a partial class, would not be caught here. The snapshot tests are the only protection.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests, which compile the output, and check that the 222 updated snapshots build without diagnostics

hunches.claim: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it allows AttributeTargets.Class on those targets (only the Assembly target was added later). The guard is therefore unnecessary, and generated code on those targets is still counted in coverage, against 'all generated code is decorated'. Ledger L7 says to follow the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Drive CSharpGeneratorDriver over a [MessagePackObject] type with CSharpParseOptions preprocessorSymbols {"NETSTANDARD2_0"}, compile the result against netstandard2.0 references, and assert that the generated formatter type symbol has ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. It fails on head because the attribute is preprocessed away even though it compiles on netstandard2.0.

hunches.claim: The guard-check test only checks that each ExcludeFromCodeCoverage occurrence is wrapped by the #if/#endif text. It never compiles the generated output for netstandard2.0, .NET Framework or modern targets. The test compilation uses default framework references and defines no NETSTANDARD2_0 symbol, so it cannot detect a wrong guard condition or macro name. Mutating the guard (e.g. NETSTANDARD2_0 -> NETSTANDARD20) would only surface if the test's own Guard constant were not also updated. The guard text is duplicated in the test, which makes the test tautological.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/FormatterTemplate.cs:33 negate-condition: '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' -> '#if NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK'; expected to survive in the new tests only if the Guard constant is not also changed, since the test hardcodes the same string and never compiles with those symbols defined

hunches.claim: The coverage test source has no generic object, nested type, or nested-resolver case. The templates have separate attribute insertions for generic formatters, nested types, CompositeResolver and its FormatterCache, and the resolver's GetFormatterHelper. The test only requires attributeCount > 0 per file and a guarded count equal to the total. Removing the attribute from FormatterCache<T> or GetFormatterHelper would still pass if the class-level attribute remains. CompositeResolverTemplate is never exercised, since the test source has no CompositeResolver generation.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/ResolverTemplate.tt:48 delete-statement: remove the guarded [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] before GetFormatterHelper; expected to survive because the test only requires >0 attributes per file with all occurrences guarded

hunches.claim: The new README text says the attribute is 'only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework)'. That implies the attribute is unavailable on those targets, which is false. The docs justify the coverage gap with an incorrect premise.

receipt_plan.detail: Look up System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute in the official .NET API docs. The 'Applies to' section lists .NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET Standard 2.0+. Compare that with README.md:1640.

hunches.claim: Only the formatter, resolver and helper types receive the attribute. Other generated types, such as the generated `GeneratedAssemblyAttribute` application or any other emitted members and helper classes, are not covered. The requirement says all generated code is to be decorated.

receipt_plan.detail: List all `class`/`struct` emissions across the Transforms templates and compare against the decorated set. Check for undecorated emitted types, for example in the resolver's GetFormatterHelper, or any other template not touched here.

residual_risk: This change touches 236 files (222 generated) in codegen-templates, tests; the highest routed risk is 7/10. 13 file(s) were routed for deep review, 1 for light review and 222 to the regeneration check. The existing source generator tests ran on head: 168 of 169 passed, 1 failed. 5 unverified hunch(es) remain without an executed receipt. 5 thing(s) were not checked, including mutation testing; compatibility byte diff (base vs head serialized bytes); A/B review branches. By signing off, the signer accepts any defect that only those unchecked paths would have revealed. The change is blocked; signing off is not offered until the blocker is fixed.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: The attribute is always emitted, with no setting. It goes on every generated formatter (int-key, string-key, enum, union), on the resolver classes and on their nested helper classes (FormatterCache, GetFormatterHelper), in the .tt templates and their regenerated .cs. Users cannot turn it off.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: The attribute is on by default, with an opt-out. Add a boolean option, e.g. an `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` property defaulting to true on GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute and its GeneratorOptions model. Each template wraps the attribute lines in `<# if (Options.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage) { #> ... <# } #>`. Snapshots are unchanged for the default, a test covers the opt-out, and the README documents the switch.
